en: The Questions of King Milinda, Chapter on Time: 9. The Discourse on Time "Venerable sir," said King Milinda, "is time eternal? "No, great king, time is not eternal. "But, venerable sir, is time impermanent? "No, great king, time is not impermanent. "But, venerable sir, is time both eternal and impermanent? "No, great king, time is neither eternal nor impermanent. "But, venerable sir, is time neither eternal nor impermanent? "No, great king, time is neither 'neither eternal nor impermanent'. "If it is asked, venerable sir, 'Is time eternal? and one says, 'No'; and if it is asked, 'Is time impermanent? and one says, 'No'; and if it is asked, 'Is time both eternal and impermanent? and one says, 'No'; and if it is asked, 'Is time neither eternal nor impermanent? and one says, 'No'—then what is time? Is it a mere word? "It is not a mere word, great king. But it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. Just as, great king, when a fire burns continuously, one speaks of 'the fire burning for a long time,' yet that fire is not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me an analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a river flows continuously, one speaks of 'the river flowing for a long time,' yet that river is not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a lamp burns continuously, one speaks of 'the lamp burning for a long time,' yet that lamp is not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a seed is sown in a field and the continuity of its growth proceeds, one speaks of 'the tree growing for a long time,' yet that tree is not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a debt is being paid back in installments, one speaks of 'the debt being paid off over a long period,' yet that debt is not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a person is traveling along a road, one speaks of 'the traveler traveling for a long time,' yet that traveler is not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a sound is produced by a succession of vibrations, one speaks of 'the sound lasting for a long time,' yet that sound is not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a mountain stream flows continuously, one speaks of 'the stream flowing for a long time,' yet that stream is not eternal;

so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a flame is passed from hand to hand, one speaks of 'the flame being carried for a long time,' yet that flame is not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a torch is whirled around, one speaks of 'a circle of fire,' yet that circle is not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a seed is planted and the continuity of its growth proceeds through sprout, stalk, leaf, and flower until the fruit is reached, one speaks of 'the tree bearing fruit after a long time,' yet that tree is not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a man is counting coins one by one, one speaks of 'the counting taking a long time,' yet those coins are not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a potter has made pots and sets them out to dry, and they are then fired, and they are then sold, and they are then used, and they are then broken, one speaks of 'the pots having been in use for a long time,' yet those pots are not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a man has a large collection of clothes and wears them one after another, one speaks of 'the man wearing the clothes for a long time,' yet those clothes are not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a man has a large collection of ornaments and wears them one after another, one speaks of 'the man wearing the ornaments for a long time,' yet those ornaments are not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a man has a large collection of musical instruments and plays them one after another, one speaks of 'the man playing the instruments for a long time,' yet those instruments are not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a man has a large collection of books and reads them one after another, one speaks of 'the man reading the books for a long time,' yet those books are not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a man has a large collection of paintings and looks at them one after another, one speaks of 'the man looking at the paintings for a long time,' yet those paintings are not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a man has a large collection of perfumes and uses them one after another, one speaks of 'the man using the perfumes for a long time,' yet those perfumes are not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a man has a large collection of foods and eats them one after another, one speaks of 'the man eating the foods for a long time,' yet those foods are not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a man has a large collection of drinks and drinks them one after another, one speaks of 'the man drinking the drinks for a long time,' yet those drinks are not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a man has a large collection of beds and sits upon them one after another, one speaks of 'the man sitting on the beds for a long time,' yet those beds are not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Give me another analogy, venerable sir. "Just as, great king, when a man has a large collection of seats and sits upon them one after another, one speaks of 'the man sitting on the seats for a long time,' yet those seats are not eternal; so too, great king, it is because of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that there is the conventional designation 'time. "Venerable Nāgasena, as for what you call 'a long period of time' (addhāna), what is this so-called 'period'?
"It is the past period, Great King, the future period, and the present period."
“But, venerable sir, do all times exist?
“Some times exist, great king, and some do not.
“But which, venerable sir, exists, and which does not?”

“Those formations, Great King, which are past, vanished, ceased, and changed—that period does not exist. Those phenomena which are results, those which are subject to result, and those which give rise to rebirth elsewhere—that period exists.
Those beings who have passed away and have arisen elsewhere—that period exists.
Those beings who have passed away and have not arisen elsewhere—that period does not exist.”
“And those beings who have attained final Nibbāna—there is no such duration [of time] because of their having attained final Nibbāna.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Chapter on Duration.
In this chapter there are nine questions.
